narratives.Overview:
1. Trust file. `.deft/approvers.json` holds a signed body `{repo, rp: {id, origins}, approvers: [{name, credentialId, publicKey, alg, aaguid, backupEligible}]}` and a proof. The first version's proof is a root: a `packed` attestation whose certificate chain verifies against vendor roots vendored in Directive (`none` and self attestation refused), plus an assertion by that credential over the body. Every later version's proof is an assertion, by a credential in the immediately preceding version, over `{schema: "deft.approvers-transition.v1", repo, predecessorDigest, bodyDigest}`; or it is a re-root by a newly attested credential that no earlier version enrolled (the lost-all-keys path; earlier records stop verifying until re-approved). A transition that leaves no attested credential in the set is refused.
2. History and stickiness. At the signed level verify walks every first-parent version of `.deft/approvers.json` from its first appearance and checks item 1 at each step. A file that appeared and is now absent or malformed refuses. A shallow clone refuses with a full-history remediation. There is no level off in this story: once opted in, a repo stays signed. `rp.id` and `origins` are part of the signed body, so moving the page is a signed change.
3. Signed payload. One canonical-encoding module (sorted keys, UTF-8, base64url) defines two domain-separated payloads, `deft.record-approval.v1` and the transition payload of item 1. A record approval is `{repo, entries}`, each entry `{kind, planId, xbriefRelPath, recordRel, changeKind, contractDigest}`, sorted and free of duplicates. Proofs sit outside the bytes they sign. The same module is bundled into the page and checked against shared test vectors.
4. Record format and verifier. At the signed level a record carries `approval: {payload, credentialId, authenticatorData, clientDataJSON, signature}`; unknown keys are refused, and the approver name is read from the credential mapping, not from the record. One helper, in the parse both evaluators share, rebuilds the record's own entry from its parsed fields, takes `repo` from `GITHUB_REPOSITORY` or the origin remote (refusing when neither resolves), requires that entry in the payload, and checks: challenge equals sha256 of the rebuilt payload; `type` is `webauthn.get`; origin in `rp.origins`; `crossOrigin` not true; `rpIdHash` equals sha256 of `rp.id`; user-present and user-verified set; signature valid under the enrolled key (ES256, RS256 and Ed25519 through `node:crypto`). It runs on the selected record only; a selected record that fails is treated as absent, so one stale record does not fail unrelated plans.
5. Ceremony page. One static page Directive ships, served from the origin named in the trust file. Approve mode decodes the set from the URL fragment, renders it as text only (strict CSP, `frame-ancestors 'none'`), computes every digest and the challenge itself, calls `navigator.credentials.get` with user verification required, and shows a result blob to copy. Enroll mode creates the new credential, builds the next trust-file body itself, shows the new credential's name, AAGUID and backup-eligible flag, and asks an enrolled key to sign the transition in the same session; it returns one combined blob. Requests above a fixed size refuse and say to split the cohort; the QR code is shown only when the link fits.
6. Verbs. At the signed level `scope:record-observable-scope` and `scope:record-intent-constraint` (one path or the cohort form) take `--request`, which builds the frozen set, prints the link and writes nothing, and `--assertion <blob>`, which rebuilds the same set, verifies the blob with the item 4 helper against the merge-base trust file, and writes exactly those records. `approvers:enroll --name <n>` (root when no trust file exists, else an add) and `approvers:remove --credential <id>` print a page link and accept only the page's combined blob. No TTY step on these paths.
7. Fallback. At the signed level a record without a valid approval (TTY-minted, hand-written, or merged by any route) is not approved. Without a trust file, and for every other mint verb, the TTY mint is unchanged.
8. Honest claim. The refusal text, both verbs' usage, `content/commands.md` and the record docs state: a valid approval proves a user-verified gesture by an enrolled authenticator over exactly this set; the human read it only if the page ran on a device the agent does not drive and was deployed with credentials the agent does not hold; Windows Hello, Touch ID, a desktop USB key and the desktop browser's cross-device QR are a lower review assurance than the phone's own browser. They also name the residuals: removing the surfaces policy, editing CI or pinning an older runtime turns the check off without forging an approval (with #6207); an approval stays valid while its key stays enrolled, so deleting a record does not revoke it and nothing expires; `approvers.json` with WebAuthn is the trust root #5862 and #6284 may reuse, and `plan.policy.onePrScopeProof` `signed` stays reserved.
9. Tests beside each changed file: valid approval; wrong key; another repo's approval pasted in; unknown origin or `rp.id`; `crossOrigin` true; UV missing; one byte changed in payload, contract, `changeKind` or plan id; an entry missing from its payload; unknown record key; a later records-only widen with the old approval; an unsigned record landed by bot merge or plain merge read at the signed level; a `--request` run writes nothing; root with `none` or self attestation; a transition by a key not in the predecessor; a re-root reusing an earlier credential; removal of the last attested credential; a rollback to an earlier version; two transitions from one predecessor; the file deleted after first appearance; a shallow clone; a stale record of plan A with a valid record of plan B; canonicalizer vectors shared with the page bundle.

## Acceptance Criteria

- With `.deft/approvers.json` at the merge base, an observable-scope or intent-constraint record is approved only when its approval verifies against a key enrolled in that file over a payload rebuilt from this repository and the record's own fields.
- A record written by hand, minted at a TTY, or merged under `DEFT_ALLOW_BOT_MERGE`, `policy:allow-bot-merge` or a plain `gh pr merge`, without a valid approval, is not approved at the signed level.
- Changing any signed record field (plan id, brief path, record path, `changeKind`, contract) requires a fresh approval; an approval from another repository does not verify.
- The first trust-file version needs a hardware attestation that verifies against the vendored roots; every later version needs an assertion by a key of its predecessor or a new attested root; deletion, rollback, a conflicting second transition and a shallow clone refuse.
- `--request` writes nothing and records carry no approval until `--assertion` verifies; the record verbs and `approvers:enroll`/`approvers:remove` need no TTY at the signed level.
- The page shows the full set, computes the challenge from the bytes it shows, and adds keys only in one session with an enrolled key's signature.
- Without a trust file, behaviour and the TTY mint are unchanged.
- The docs and refusal text state what a valid approval proves and the named residuals.

One helper, in the parse both evaluators share, rebuilds the record's own entry from its parsed fields, takes `repo` from `GITHUB_REPOSITORY` or the origin remote (refusing when neither resolves), requires that entry in the payload, and checks: challenge equals sha256 of the rebuilt payload; `type` is `webauthn.get`; origin in `rp.origins`; `crossOrigin` not true; `rpIdHash` equals sha256 of `rp.id`; user-present and user-verified set; signature valid under the enrolled key (ES256, RS256 and Ed25519 through `node:crypto`). It runs on the selected record only; a selected record that fails is treated as absent, so one stale record does not fail unrelated plans.

Ceremony page. One static page Directive ships, served from the origin named in the trust file. Approve mode decodes the set from the URL fragment, renders it as text only (strict CSP, `frame-ancestors 'none'`), computes every digest and the challenge itself, calls `navigator.credentials.get` with user verification required, and shows a result blob to copy. Enroll mode creates the new credential, builds the next trust-file body itself, shows the new credential's name, AAGUID and backup-eligible flag, and asks an enrolled key to sign the transition in the same session; it returns one combined blob. Requests above a fixed size refuse and say to split the cohort; the QR code is shown only when the link fits.

Verbs. At the signed level `scope:record-observable-scope` and `scope:record-intent-constraint` (one path or the cohort form) take `--request`, which builds the frozen set, prints the link and writes nothing, and `--assertion <blob>`, which rebuilds the same set, verifies the blob with the item 4 helper against the merge-base trust file, and writes exactly those records. `approvers:enroll --name <n>` (root when no trust file exists, else an add) and `approvers:remove --credential <id>` print a page link and accept only the page's combined blob. No TTY step on these paths.

Fallback. At the signed level a record without a valid approval (TTY-minted, hand-written, or merged by any route) is not approved. Without a trust file, and for every other mint verb, the TTY mint is unchanged.

Honest claim. The refusal text, both verbs' usage, `content/commands.md` and the record docs state: a valid approval proves a user-verified gesture by an enrolled authenticator over exactly this set; the human read it only if the page ran on a device the agent does not drive and was deployed with credentials the agent does not hold; Windows Hello, Touch ID, a desktop USB key and the desktop browser's cross-device QR are a lower review assurance than the phone's own browser. They also name the residuals: removing the surfaces policy, editing CI or pinning an older runtime turns the check off without forging an approval (with #6207); an approval stays valid while its key stays enrolled, so deleting a record does not revoke it and nothing expires; `approvers.json` with WebAuthn is the trust root #5862 and #6284 may reuse, and `plan.policy.onePrScopeProof` `signed` stays reserved.

Tests beside each changed file: valid approval; wrong key; another repo's approval pasted in; unknown origin or `rp.id`; `crossOrigin` true; UV missing; one byte changed in payload, contract, `changeKind` or plan id; an entry missing from its payload; unknown record key; a later records-only widen with the old approval; an unsigned record landed by bot merge or plain merge read at the signed level; a `--request` run writes nothing; root with `none` or self attestation; a transition by a key not in the predecessor; a re-root reusing an earlier credential; removal of the last attested credential; a rollback to an earlier version; two transitions from one predecessor; the file deleted after first appearance; a shallow clone; a stale record of plan A with a valid record of plan B; canonicalizer vectors shared with the page bundle.

With `.deft/approvers.json` at the merge base, an observable-scope or intent-constraint record is approved only when its approval verifies against a key enrolled in that file over a payload rebuilt from this repository and the record's own fields.
A record written by hand, minted at a TTY, or merged under `DEFT_ALLOW_BOT_MERGE`, `policy:allow-bot-merge` or a plain `gh pr merge`, without a valid approval, is not approved at the signed level.
Changing any signed record field (plan id, brief path, record path, `changeKind`, contract) requires a fresh approval; an approval from another repository does not verify.

The first trust-file version needs a hardware attestation that verifies against the vendored roots; every later version needs an assertion by a key of its predecessor or a new attested root; deletion, rollback, a conflicting second transition and a shallow clone refuse.
`--request` writes nothing and records carry no approval until `--assertion` verifies; the record verbs and `approvers:enroll`/`approvers:remove` need no TTY at the signed level.
The page shows the full set, computes the challenge from the bytes it shows, and adds keys only in one session with an enrolled key's signature.
Without a trust file, behaviour and the TTY mint are unchanged.
The docs and refusal text state what a valid approval proves and the named residuals.

## In plain English

The problem is approving work from a phone without letting an agent manufacture that approval using the operator’s credentials. WebAuthn can supply a useful signature, but **R1–R10 cannot bind as written**: the proposed bootstrap and recovery can install an agent-controlled key, deleting the trust file restores unsigned approval, and the authenticator does not prove that the human saw the content it signed.

Short answers to the nine questions:

1. **No, not yet.** R2–R3 can prevent changed-content replay after a trustworthy key is enrolled. They do not establish trustworthy enrollment, protect the approval page, or prevent rollback of trust configuration.
2. **Fragment and paste-back is viable for bounded requests.** Full cohorts need an explicit size limit and file-import alternative. Localhost adds another origin and does not solve remote phone access. A dedicated, independently administered HTTPS origin is the clearest first choice; self-hosting means owning its deployment security and credential lifecycle.
3. **TTY bootstrap is insufficient for the stated adversary.** Initial trust needs an independently authenticated root or an explicit trusted, agent-free provisioning assumption. Attestation can constrain authenticator provenance; it does not establish which human may authorize this repository.
4. **Invalidating removed-key records is coherent**, with an explicit current-authority model. Ordinary revocation must not destroy the historical evidence authorizing later keys. Losing every key must fail closed unless an independently anchored recovery authority exists.
5. **One approver is reasonable initially.** An existing approver may authorize another key, but that means trusting the new key’s custody. A signed enrollment alone does not prove it is hardware-held or requires a human.
6. **Authorization-field signing can suffice for authority, but does not satisfy literal whole-file byte equality.** The schema must define every covered field and normalization rule. Independent sibling verification means approval of individual entries, not an indivisible cohort.
7. **An inline chain helps shallow clones but does not establish its own root or freshness.** Deletion, rollback and replacement need protection outside the mutable file.
8. **Yes:** TTY-only fallback can remain in unsigned repositories. At the signed level it cannot grant authority unless it produces the same independently verifiable proof.
9. **This adds refusals and network dependencies.** Signature, enrollment, trust-transition, recovery and malformed-request checks are new refusals. The hosted ceremony needs network access; Git-history verification may require fetching history. Offline signature checking itself needs neither forge nor network access.

The smallest useful end-to-end slice is one record approved on a phone, using a fixed independently provisioned trust configuration, a dedicated approval page, a canonical authorization envelope, and verification in both record consumers. Cohorts can follow using the existing frozen-set machinery. Dynamic enrollment chains, all-keys-lost recovery, self-hosted origins, localhost, commit fetching, thresholds and broad authenticator compatibility should be separate slices. A verifier-only first PR is buildable infrastructure, but does not relieve the phone-approval pain.

All repository evidence below was read at `07a7ac44ee8c5cce48510e05ec8f9ad40ca28203`. WebAuthn statements are protocol knowledge, not repository findings or browser-tested claims; no web access was used.

### 1. blocks-the-design — Bootstrap and recovery cannot authenticate their own trust root

**Evidence:** `packages/runtime/src/human-presence-mint.ts:22–88` describes environment markers, TTY checks and a typed phrase. `packages/core/src/scope-provenance/digest.ts:231–252` accepts human-looking strings. `packages/core/src/authz/protected-dest-realpath.ts:20–32` protects authz and approved-scope stores, not the proposed approver store. R5 and R6 rely on that TTY process for first enrollment and total-loss recovery.

**Failure:** An agent generates a software key pair, fabricates registration data, writes an initial approvers file and lands it under shared forge credentials. A verifier walking back to that first file has no evidence that the TTY ceremony occurred. The software signer can construct assertions with UP and UV bits set; those bits are meaningful only when the enrolled key and authenticator implementation are trusted. Resetting through the same bootstrap after “all keys lost” repeats the attack.

An existing approver signing a later enrollment also authorizes the supplied public key, not a demonstrated hardware custody property. Without verified attestation or a trusted enrollment ceremony, that key can likewise be software-generated.

**Consequence:** R5–R6 need an external trust anchor and an explicit enrollment assurance model. Initial provisioning may be a trusted administrative act outside agent reach; recovery may use a separately provisioned recovery key. An unverifiable TTY claim or ordinary PR merge cannot establish either boundary. Attestation is an optional restriction on supported authenticators, not a universal solution compatible with every synced passkey.

### 2. blocks-the-design — An absent trust file permits downgrade, and a valid chain permits rollback

**Evidence:** R1 makes absence equivalent to today’s behavior. At the pinned SHA, `observable-scope/evaluate.ts:390–425` and `intent-constraint/evaluate.ts:522–541`, under `packages/core/src/`, return N/A before record checks on relevant metadata-only changes. R3 proposes integrating verification into those consumers; R5 specifies history validation but no independently retained latest state.

**Failure:** A record-only administrative PR deletes `approvers.json`. The next product PR sees absence and admits the unsigned path. Alternatively, an agent restores an older, genuinely signed approver state containing a revoked key. A chain can be cryptographically valid while stale. An inline chain changes availability, not this security property.

Concurrent rotations also need a defined predecessor: two updates signed against the same old state must not silently overwrite one another’s revocations.

**Consequence:** Opt-in needs a persistent enforcement anchor that absence cannot erase, plus authenticated predecessor binding and rollback protection for trust transitions. Administrative changes must be checked even when no UI or production file changes. Shallow history must produce a clear refusal or use a complete supplied chain rooted at the independent anchor; it cannot become fresh bootstrap. The design must state the trusted execution boundary for the verifier and its configuration.

### 3. blocks-the-design — A WebAuthn gesture does not attest to the displayed approval

**Evidence:** Protocol knowledge: an assertion signs authenticator data and the hash of `clientDataJSON`, which includes the challenge and origin. Ordinary WebAuthn does not provide a trusted display of the application’s arbitrary transaction content. R4 relies on page code to connect the displayed records to the challenge; R9 relies on a banner and credential naming.

**Failure:** Page code deployed using credentials available to the agent displays benign set A while requesting a signature over broader set B. Browser automation with script-execution access can create the same mismatch on an otherwise legitimate origin. All R3 signature checks still pass. A hardware key or a phone used only as the desktop browser’s cross-device authenticator does not independently show and validate the complete record set.

The fragment is not included in the HTTP request, but page JavaScript can read and transmit it. “Never sent to a server” is therefore a property of trusted page code, not a protection afforded by fragments alone.

**Consequence:** R4 requires a trusted renderer and deployment boundary outside the agent’s credentials and browser control. Phone-native review in an independently controlled browser is a defensible initial ceremony under that explicit assumption. Desktop Hello, Touch ID and cross-device authentication can remain compatible authentication mechanisms, but cannot be advertised as equivalent transaction-review assurance. A banner does not repair this boundary.

The strongest argument for R4 is that a small static application minimizes backend trust and permits offline verification. That is useful. The verdict changes when control of that application’s delivered code and the reviewing browser is explicitly outside the adversary’s capabilities.

Problem: before an agent may change visible UI or add a production constraint, a human approves a record (`.deft/observable-scope/`, `.deft/intent-constraint/`). It also proves nothing: the stamp is checked for shape only, the folders are not guarded, and the merge that lands a record can be the agent's own.

What the three critics found: a WebAuthn signature from an enrolled key is the right tool, and the record check itself is sound. But the Stop 1 design could not bind. The list of enrolled keys started from a file an agent could write and merge, or enroll through a terminal gate an agent can fake. Deleting the file switched the repo back to the old shape check. Enrolling a key passed through the agent, which could swap in its own key. The signed payload trusted a copy stored in the record, so an approval from another repo could be pasted in. And the page cannot prove that the human saw what was signed: on the dev machine an agent that drives the browser can show one set and request a signature over another.

Solution this lean proposes: the first enrolled key must be a hardware security key whose registration carries a manufacturer attestation that the verifier checks against vendor roots shipped with Directive. An agent cannot fake that. Phone passkeys, Windows Hello and Touch ID join later, added by an already enrolled key in one page session that shows the new key. Every change to the key list is signed by a key already on it, and verify walks the file's history, so deleting the file, rolling it back or replacing it refuses. Records are approved through one static page that receives the whole set in its link, shows it, hashes it and asks for the signature; the operator pastes the result back and the agent writes the records. Verify rebuilds what was signed from this repository and the record's own fields. At the signed level a record without a valid signature is not approved, however it was merged.

What a valid signature proves: an enrolled authenticator made a user-verified gesture over exactly that set. It does not prove the human read the set. That holds when the page runs on a device the agent does not drive, such as the phone's own browser, and the page is deployed with credentials the agent does not hold. The docs say so.

What this adds: two verbs (`approvers:enroll`, `approvers:remove`), `--request` and `--assertion` on the two record verbs, and new refusals at the signed level only: a record without a valid signature, a broken or missing key list, a shallow clone, and an oversized request. No forge read and no network read in verify. Repos that do not opt in keep today's terminal mint.

What it does not do: Windows Hello or Apple attestation for the first key, a device-bound key policy, k-of-n approvals, leaving the signed level, record expiry, revoking one specific approval, a localhost page, and reuse by #5862 or #6284. Those are later stories.
If confirmed, the synthesis would assert this design.

## Bound remedy
1. Trust file. `.deft/approvers.json` holds a signed body `{repo, rp: {id, origins}, approvers: [{name, credentialId, publicKey, alg, aaguid, backupEligible}]}` and a proof. The first version's proof is a root: a `packed` attestation whose certificate chain verifies against vendor roots vendored in Directive (`none` and self attestation refused), plus an assertion by that credential over the body. Every later version's proof is an assertion, by a credential in the immediately preceding version, over `{schema: "deft.approvers-transition.v1", repo, predecessorDigest, bodyDigest}`; or it is a re-root by a newly attested credential that no earlier version enrolled (the lost-all-keys path; earlier records stop verifying until re-approved). A transition that leaves no attested credential in the set is refused.
2. History and stickiness. At the signed level verify walks every first-parent version of `.deft/approvers.json` from its first appearance and checks item 1 at each step. A file that appeared and is now absent or malformed refuses. A shallow clone refuses with a full-history remediation. There is no level off in this story: once opted in, a repo stays signed. `rp.id` and `origins` are part of the signed body, so moving the page is a signed change.
3. Signed payload. One canonical-encoding module (sorted keys, UTF-8, base64url) defines two domain-separated payloads, `deft.record-approval.v1` and the transition payload of item 1. A record approval is `{repo, entries}`, each entry `{kind, planId, xbriefRelPath, recordRel, changeKind, contractDigest}`, sorted and free of duplicates. Proofs sit outside the bytes they sign. The same module is bundled into the page and checked against shared test vectors.
4. Record format and verifier. At the signed level a record carries `approval: {payload, credentialId, authenticatorData, clientDataJSON, signature}`; unknown keys are refused, and the approver name is read from the credential mapping, not from the record. One helper, in the parse both evaluators share, rebuilds the record's own entry from its parsed fields, takes `repo` from `GITHUB_REPOSITORY` or the origin remote (refusing when neither resolves), requires that entry in the payload, and checks: challenge equals sha256 of the rebuilt payload; `type` is `webauthn.get`; origin in `rp.origins`; `crossOrigin` not true; `rpIdHash` equals sha256 of `rp.id`; user-present and user-verified set; signature valid under the enrolled key (ES256, RS256 and Ed25519 through `node:crypto`). It runs on the selected record only; a selected record that fails is treated as absent, so one stale record does not fail unrelated plans.
5. Ceremony page. One static page Directive ships, served from the origin named in the trust file. Approve mode decodes the set from the URL fragment, renders it as text only (strict CSP, `frame-ancestors 'none'`), computes every digest and the challenge itself, calls `navigator.credentials.get` with user verification required, and shows a result blob to copy. Enroll mode creates the new credential, builds the next trust-file body itself, shows the new credential's name, AAGUID and backup-eligible flag, and asks an enrolled key to sign the transition in the same session; it returns one combined blob. Requests above a fixed size refuse and say to split the cohort; the QR code is shown only when the link fits.
